title: Syntax and Semantics in Propositional Logic

blocks.text: Propositional logic forms the backbone of logical reasoning in computer science and mathematics. Understanding its syntax and semantics is essential for constructing and evaluating logical arguments.

blocks.markdown: In propositional logic, we work with statements that can be either true or false. These statements are called propositions. The syntax of propositional logic involves constructing well-formed formulae (WFFs) using logical connectives such as \( \land \) (and), \( \lor \) (or), \( \lnot \) (not), and \( \rightarrow \) (implies).

blocks.title: Well-formed Formula (WFF)
blocks.text: A well-formed formula is a string of symbols that is constructed according to the rules of the grammar of propositional logic.

blocks.markdown:
To determine if a formula is well-formed, we need to ensure that it adheres to the syntax rules. A formula is well-formed if:
- Every propositional variable is a WFF.
- If \( \phi \) and \( \psi \) are WFFs, then \( \lnot \phi \), \( (\phi \land \psi) \), \( (\phi \lor \psi) \), and \( (\phi \rightarrow \psi) \) are also WFFs.

blocks.title: Identifying Well-formed Formulae
blocks.prompt: Determine if the following formula is well-formed: \( (p \land (q \lor \lnot r)) \)

steps.text: Identify the atomic propositions: \( p \), \( q \), and \( r \).
Check the innermost expression: \( (q \lor \lnot r) \) is a WFF since \( q \) and \( \lnot r \) are WFFs.
Check the entire formula: \( (p \land (q \lor \lnot r)) \) is a WFF since both \( p \) and \( (q \lor \lnot r) \) are WFFs.

blocks.markdown: Next, we explore the semantics of propositional logic, which involves assigning truth values to propositions and evaluating the truth of formulae. A valuation is a function that assigns a truth value (true or false) to each propositional variable.

blocks.title: Valuation
blocks.text: A valuation \( v \) is a function from the set of propositional variables to \( \{ \text{true}, \text{false} \} \).

blocks.title: Evaluating a Formula
blocks.prompt: Evaluate the formula \( (p \rightarrow q) \) under the valuation \( v(p) = \text{true}, v(q) = \text{false} \).

steps.text: Recall the truth table for implication: \( p \rightarrow q \) is false only when \( p \) is true and \( q \) is false.
Apply the truth table: Since \( p \) is true and \( q \) is false, \( (p \rightarrow q) \) evaluates to false.

blocks.answer: The formula \( (p \rightarrow q) \) evaluates to false under the given valuation.

blocks.markdown: A formula is satisfiable if there exists at least one valuation that makes the formula true. It is valid if it is true under all valuations, and unsatisfiable if there is no valuation that makes it true.

blocks.title: Satisfiability and Validity
blocks.text: A formula is satisfiable if there exists a valuation that makes it true. It is valid if it is true under all valuations, and unsatisfiable if no valuation makes it true.

points: A well-formed formula (WFF) is constructed according to specific syntax rules.
Valuation assigns truth values to propositions, allowing evaluation of formulae.
A formula can be satisfiable, valid, or unsatisfiable based on its truth under different valuations.
